## Why This Is Asked

```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: policy-watcher Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: policy-watcher
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
      - name: pods-pvc
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pods-pvc
      - name: policies
        configMap:
          name: policy-config
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools

        command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache yq jq"]

        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: api-creds
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pods-pvc
          mountPath: /pods
        - name: policies
          mountPath: /policies
```

- How would you test this in CI for policy regressions?
- What happens when policy-config changes at runtime?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement a practical, namespace-scoped canary upgrade using standard CKAD tools: CronJob scheduling, patching Deployments, ConfigMaps/Secrets for config and credentials, and PVC-based logging. It also exercises InitContainers, probes, and network policy considerations in a real workflow.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scheduling and JobTemplate execution
- Patching Deployment images with kubectl set image or patch
- Reading image tag from ConfigMap and registry authentication via Secret
- Persisting status in a ConfigMap and logging to a PVC
- InitContainer to install tooling (kubectl, jq)
- Readiness/Liveness probes for the Job Pod
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting registry egress

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-upgrade
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: canary-sa
          initContainers:
          - name: install-tools
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq; true"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          containers:
          - name: upgrader
            image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "set -e; CANARY_TAG=$(kubectl get configmap canary-config -o jsonpath='{.data.tag}'); kubectl patch deployment my-app -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"my-app","image":"myrepo/my-app:${CANARY_TAG}"}]}}}}' --record; echo done; sleep 1"]
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          imagePullSecrets:
          - name: registry-credentials
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How to implement idempotent patches and roll back on failure?
- How to measure canary success (latency, error rate) before full rollout?
- How would this scale across many namespaces or deployments?

## Why This Is Asked
Assesses practical CKAD skills: CronJob/Job TTL, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, PVCs, probes, RBAC, and NetworkPolicy with a realistic data-pruning task.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob and TTLAfterFinished
- InitContainer to stage scripts
- ConfigMap-driven parameters
- PVC mounting
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- RBAC least privilege via ServiceAccount
- NetworkPolicy egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: data-pruner
spec:
  schedule: "0 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: analytics-pruner
          initContainers:
          - name: stage-script
            image: busybox
            command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /scripts/prune.sh /prune.sh"]
          containers:
          - name: prune
            image: alpine:3.18
            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/prune.sh"]
            resources:
              requests:
                memory: "64Mi"
                cpu: "100m"
              limits:
                memory: "128Mi"
                cpu: "250m"
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: data
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: dumps-pvc
          - name: scripts
            configMap:
              name: prune-scripts
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test TTLAfterFinished behavior in a staging cluster?
- What monitoring would you add for prune activity and failure retry logic?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests CKAD proficiency across namespace-scoped automation, ConfigMap manipulation, InitContainers, and secure egress controls in real-world migration workflows.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob scoped to a namespace with per-namespace behavior
- InitContainer to install tooling (yq) and prepare environment
- ConfigMap-driven migration plan and idempotent updates
- PVC-backed logs and a Secret-backed external POST
- Readiness/Liveness probes for resilient Jobs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to the migration portal

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: per-namespace CronJob migrating ConfigMaps
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: config-migrate
  namespace: target-namespace
spec:
  schedule: "0 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: migrate-sa
          initContainers:
          - name: installer
            image: alpine:3.17
            command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache go && go install github.com/mikefarah/yq@latest"]
          containers:
          - name: migrate
            image: my-registry/config-migrate:latest
            envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: migration-api
            volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              httpGet:
                path: /healthz
                port: 8080
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: logs-pvc
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotent migrations across runs?
- How would you handle partial failures or large numbers of ConfigMaps?
- What monitoring would you add to detect drift or failures?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design Kubernetes-native backup patterns using CRD + Job orchestration, with proper use of InitContainers, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and PVs. Encourages thinking about per-namespace scoping, fault-tolerance, and minimal operator logic.

## Key Concepts
- CustomResourceDefinition and a namespace-scoped controller
- Jobs, InitContainers, and data packaging (tarball) for backups
- Secrets for credentials and ConfigMaps for configuration
- PVC usage for temporary/log data and readiness/liveness probes
- Idempotency, retries, and failure semantics

## Trade-offs Discussion

**Advantages:**
- Namespace isolation prevents cross-namespace interference
- Job-based approach provides built-in retry and failure handling
- InitContainers ensure dependencies are met before main workload
- Readiness/liveness probes provide operational visibility
- Secret/ConfigMap separation follows security best practices

**Limitations:**
- Requires custom controller for CRD watching and Job creation
- No incremental backup support (full tarball each time)
- AWS credentials stored in cluster (consider IRSA/EKS)
- No backup verification or restore automation
- PVC mounting requires proper permissions and access

**Alternatives:**
- Use Velero for comprehensive backup/restore solution
- Implement CSI snapshot for instant PVC backups
- Consider sidecar pattern for continuous backup
- Use CronJob instead of one-time Jobs for scheduled backups

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: healer
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: healer
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: health-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests real-world container orchestration patterns: InitContainers for bootstrap, sidecar for log shipping, shared volumes for cross-container data, and proper health checks plus rollback strategy.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer for pre-boot config
- Shared volumes and proper MountPaths
- Sidecar pattern for log shipping
- Readiness and Liveness probes tailored to production workloads
- Rollback strategy and safe deploys

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal patch sketch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: processor
  namespace: payments
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: fix-permissions
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "chown -R 1000:1000 /mnt/logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /mnt/logs
      containers:
      - name: processor
        image: your-registry/processor:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: in-data
          mountPath: /data/input
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/processor
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 8080
      - name: log-shipper
        image: busybox:stable
        command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -F /var/log/processor/app.log | nc log-collector 10514"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/processor
        - name: ship
          mountPath: /var/log/ship
      volumes:
      - name: in-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: processor-input-pvc
      - name: logs
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: ship
        emptyDir: {}
      restartPolicy: Always
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate zero-downtime rollouts with this setup? 
- How would you monitor and retry failed log shipments without impacting processor throughput?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Static-site serving in a per-namespace context tests PVC/ConfigMap/Secret integration, nginx config via ConfigMap, and safe multi-tenant limits with quotas and limits.

## Key Concepts

- Deployments, replicas, and rolling updates
- PVCs for shared data, ConfigMaps for content and nginx.conf, Secrets for credentials
- nginx basic auth integration via config map
- ClusterIP Service exposure and Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace ResourceQuota and LimitRange for multi-tenant safety

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal skeleton showing core resources
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: site-content
data:
  index.html: |-
    <html>...</html>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-config
data:
  nginx.conf: |
    server { listen 80; location / { auth_basic "Restricted"; auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/.htpasswd; root /usr/share/nginx/html; } }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: basic-auth
type: Opaque
data:
  # base64(encoded username:password)
  htpasswd: <base64>
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-site
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:stable
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: site
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
          subPath: nginx.conf
        - name: auth
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/.htpasswd
          subPath: htpasswd
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: site
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: static-site-pvc
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: nginx-config
      - name: auth
        secret:
          secretName: basic-auth
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: static-site-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: static-site
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    protocol: TCP
  type: ClusterIP
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: static-site-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you update content without downtime?
- How would you rotate credentials and reflect it in nginx without redeploying pods?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: PVC handling, InitContainers, ConfigMaps/Secrets, simple templating, manifest validation, and network policies. It avoids previous questions by focusing on label injection and re-validation flow.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer tool installation (kubeval, yamllint)
- ConfigMap/Secret usage for config and credentials
- PVC-mounted manifest discovery and simple file loop
- Lightweight templating to inject labels
- Validation with kubeval/yamllint and conditional POST
- TLS sidecar and readiness/liveness probes
- Namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: manifest-tagger
  namespace: <target-namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: manifest-tagger
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache kubeval yamllint curl jq && echo done"]
      containers:
      - name: tagger
        image: your-registry/manifest-tagger:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /manifests
        - name: tagged
          mountPath: /tagged
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config
        env:
        - name: TAG_KEY
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: tagger-config
              key: tag-key
        - name: API_BASE
          value: http://tagger-portal:8080/api/v1/summary
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: curlimages/curl:7.88.1
        # TLS rotation logic assumed
      volumes:
      - name: manifests
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: manifests-pvc
      - name: tagged
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: tagger-config
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Auditors assess knowledge of Kubernetes pod security hardening and defense-in-depth strategies.

## Key Concepts
- Pod securityContext vs container securityContext
- runAsNonRoot enforcement and UID requirements
- readOnlyRootFilesystem and volume mount implications
- Capability dropping and privilege escalation controls
- Seccomp profiles via annotations and runtime defaults
- Rolling update safety and rollback procedures

## Code Example
```yaml
# Security hardening patch for collector Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod: runtime/default
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 2000
      containers:
      - name: collector
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop:
            - ALL
          volumeMounts:
          - name: input
            mountPath: /data/input
          - name: output
            mountPath: /data/output
        # Preserve existing probes and resources
        # livenessProbe, readinessProbe, resources remain unchanged
```

## Validation & Rollback
**Validation:**
- `kubectl get pods -n apps -l app=collector -o yaml | grep securityContext`
- `kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:apps:collector`
- Test pod startup and volume access
- Verify non-root execution: `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- id`

**Rollback:**
- `kubectl rollout undo deployment/collector -n apps`
- Monitor rollout status: `kubectl rollout status deployment/collector -n apps`
- Document security context changes in version control

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical CKAD skills: autoscaling, robustness, and upgrade safety in real workloads.

## Key Concepts

- Deployment resources and probes
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler (autoscale on CPU)
- PodDisruptionBudget for maintenance safety
- Observability: kubectl top, metrics-server

## Code Example

```yaml
# Deployment patch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: collector:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 15
```

```yaml
# HPA
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: collector-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: collector
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
```

```yaml
# PodDisruptionBudget
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: collector-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: collector
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you verify HPA behavior under a synthetic load step?
- What changes if workloads are bursty and you want per-pod CPU caps?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Assesses ability to choreograph ephemeral canaries using core CKAD primitives: templated Deployment from ConfigMap, secret-based auth, logs via PVC, init containers, probes, and namespace-scoped NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- ConfigMap templating for Deployment
- Secret-based API tokens and restricted RBAC
- PVC-backed logs and cleanup discipline
- InitContainers for tooling bootstrap
- Readiness/Liveness probes for short-lived canaries
- NetworkPolicy scoped to external dashboard

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-tester
spec:
  schedule: "*/20 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
            - name: install-tools
              image: alpine:3.18
              command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
          containers:
            - name: canary
              image: my-canary-image:latest
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/canary/run.sh"]
              env:
                - name: DASHBOARD_TOKEN
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: canary-token
                      key: token
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: canary-logs
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you rollback a failing canary and propagate the status to the dashboard?
- What are the memory/CPU considerations for rapid-canary spikes and how would you cap them?
